paragraphs.heading: A mouth in the leaf
paragraphs.text: A stoma is a pore in the skin, or epidermis, of a leaf, a stem or another plant organ. Its name comes from the Greek word for mouth, and the plural is stomata. Each pore sits between a pair of specialised cells called guard cells, which make the opening wider or narrower. In this way the plant controls how fast gases pass between the air spaces inside the leaf and the outside air. The word usually means the whole unit: the two guard cells plus the opening, called the stomatal aperture.

paragraphs.heading: Gaining air, losing water
paragraphs.text: Air passes through stomata by gaseous diffusion. That air brings carbon dioxide, which the plant uses in photosynthesis, and oxygen, which it uses in respiration. The air spaces inside a leaf are saturated with water vapour, and that vapour diffuses out through the same pores, a loss called transpiration. So a plant cannot take in carbon dioxide without giving up water vapour at the same time.

paragraphs.heading: Where stomata sit
paragraphs.text: Nearly all land plants have stomata in their sporophyte generation; liverworts lack them, as do some mosses and hornworts. In vascular plants their number, size and placement vary a great deal. Dicotyledons usually carry more on the lower side of a leaf than the upper side, while monocotyledons such as onion, oat and maize may have roughly equal numbers on both. Most trees have them on the underside alone, and floating leaves may have them only on top. A single stoma measures between 10 and 80 μm from end to end.

paragraphs.heading: Why the pores open wide
paragraphs.text: Inside the leaf, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide to ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate, or RuBP. RuBisCO has a fairly low affinity for carbon dioxide, and it also fixes oxygen to RuBP, which throws away energy and carbon in a process called photorespiration. Both problems mean it needs plenty of carbon dioxide, so the stomata must open wide and the plant loses a lot of water. Some plants add a helper molecule, PEPcase, which grips carbon dioxide strongly and lets the pores stay narrower. Getting the fixed carbon back from PEPcase costs a lot of energy, so it pays off only where water is scarce but light is plentiful, or where heat makes RuBisCO's oxygen problem worse.

paragraphs.heading: Plants that breathe at night
paragraphs.text: Crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM, is the trick of a group of mostly desert plants. They open their pores at night, when leaves lose water to evaporation more slowly, fix carbon dioxide with PEPcase and store the products in large vacuoles. Next day the pores stay shut, and the stored carbon dioxide is released to RuBisCO, which keeps photorespiration to a minimum. The amount a plant can store limits the method, so it pays off only when water is severely short. Most plants lack CAM and must open and close their stomata by day as light, humidity and carbon dioxide levels change.

paragraphs.heading: How guard cells open
paragraphs.text: In good conditions, such as bright light and high humidity, a proton pump pushes hydrogen ions (H⁺) out of the guard cells, so their electrical potential grows more negative. That opens channels which let potassium ions (K⁺) in, and their charge is balanced by chloride ions or by malate made in the cell. With more dissolved material inside, water moves in by osmosis, and the cells swell with turgor pressure. Rings of cellulose microfibrils stop the guard cells from getting wider, and their ends are held by neighbouring cells. So the two cells grow longer and bow apart, opening the pore.

paragraphs.heading: Closing in a drought
paragraphs.text: When roots sense that the soil is short of water, a substance called abscisic acid, or ABA, is released. ABA binds to receptors in the guard cells, raising the pH of their cytosol and the level of free calcium ions (Ca²⁺) there. Chloride and organic ions then leave the cells, and potassium stops coming in and starts to flow out. Losing these solutes sends water back out by osmosis, the cells become plasmolysed, and the pores close.
